cues.en: OK, so there's a well-known problem for speakers at conferences like these. DevCon's a big place. People are spread out. People are still coming and going. And at the beginning of your talk, probably there's still people coming in. Everyone hasn't really made it yet. And so what speakers do is they try and start slow so that nobody misses any of the interesting stuff. So they'll start with a tedious bio about their background or go into the history of the problem that they're going to be talking about.
cues.zh: 好，像这类大会的演讲者都会遇到一个常见的问题。DevCon 场地很大，大家分散在各处，人流进进出出。在你刚开讲的时候，可能还有人正走进来，大家还没完全到齐。所以演讲者通常会先放慢节奏，免得有人错过精彩内容。他们一般会先念一段冗长乏味的个人履历，或者讲讲今天要聊的问题的历史背景。

cues.en: But I don't really like that stuff. So I want to try something a little different, or I'm just going to tell, for the first three minutes here, a completely unrelated, totally random story that has nothing to do with computer security or this talk. Here it goes. The story goes like this. OK, so just after I'd gotten out of high school, me and some friends had this hair-breaking scheme where we thought that we were going to travel to the Caribbean.
cues.zh: 但我不太喜欢那一套。所以我想换个花样，在这开头的头三分钟里，讲一个完全不相干、随手拈来的故事，跟计算机安全或者本场演讲毫无关系。事情是这样的。那是我刚高中毕业的时候，我和几个朋友脑子一热，策划了一个异想天开的计划，想去加勒比海，

cues.en: find an uninhabited island and colonize it. Yes, I know. I blame DDSE on my youth. So this is a long time ago, and back then driving was cheaper than flying. So we drove all the way to Miami before getting on an airplane for a short flight into the Caribbean, where we tried to find a boat, et cetera. And it didn't really work out, obviously. We were very hungry.
cues.zh: 找一座无人岛并占领它。是的，我知道很离谱。我把这归咎于当年年轻无知。那是很久以前的事了，当时开车比坐飞机便宜。于是我们一路开到迈阿密，然后再搭短途航班飞到加勒比，试图在那儿找条船什么的。显然，这事最后没成。当时我们饿得要命。

cues.en: And so then on the way back, we were driving back up north through Florida, feeling somewhat defeated. And we decided to stop for lunch at some point. And we actually wanted to stop and get out of the car, so we saw this kind of Tex-Mex-type restaurant, the kind of place with ships, and you sit down, that kind of thing. So we stopped, and we got out of the car, and we started walking towards this restaurant. And through the parking lot, about halfway there,
cues.zh: 然后返程时，我们开车北上穿过佛罗里达，感觉有点挫败。我们决定找个地方停下来吃午饭。其实我们想下车活动活动，就看到一家有点像德州墨西哥风味的餐厅，那种带帆船装饰、可以坐下来慢慢吃的地方。于是我们停下车，走出来，朝那家餐厅走去。穿过停车场，走到一半左右，

cues.en: I was with two friends, and one of them realized that he'd left something in the car or that he'd left it unlocked or something like that. So he turned around and went back to the car while my other friend and I went into the restaurant. And when we got into the restaurant, we caught the end of their birthday ritual. I feel like these restaurants all have their own sort of unique birthday ritual. They have a special song or something that they sing when people come out. And so we caught the end of theirs. And it was the strangest thing I've ever seen in a restaurant.
cues.zh: 我当时和两个朋友在一起，其中一个发现他把什么东西落在车里了，或者车没锁之类的。于是他转身回车上去，而我和另一个朋友先进了餐厅。我们进餐厅的时候，正好赶上他们生日仪式的尾声。我觉得这类餐厅都有自己独特的生日仪式，会唱一首特别的歌什么的，有人过生日就唱。我们正好赶上了他们的尾声，那是我在餐厅里见过的最诡异的场面。

cues.en: So they came out, you know, singing and there's two waiters and one of them stood in front of the woman whose birthday it was with a little like saucer, you know, plate type, you know, almost like you put a teacup on it with just a little dab of whipped cream on it and a spoon and held it in front of her and asked her to close her eyes and open her mouth as if he was going to feed her this whipped cream. Meanwhile, there was another waiter standing behind her with a full pie tin full of whipped cream.
cues.zh: 他们出来了，唱着歌，有两个服务员，其中一个站在过生日的女士面前，手里拿着一个小碟子，像茶托那种，几乎就是放茶杯的那种，上面只有一小坨打发奶油和一把勺子，举到她面前，让她闭上眼睛张开嘴，好像要喂她吃那坨奶油。与此同时，另一个服务员站在她身后，端着一个装满打发奶油的派盘。

cues.en: And she closed her eyes and opened her mouth, and the dude reaches around and just slams her in the face with the whipped cream, you know? I mean, this lady's shocked, you know, it's her birthday, she's dressed up, she just gets like a pie to the face, you know? No warning at all. And so my friend and I are standing there, like, you know, looking at this, you know, Mal's open, and my other friend is still at the car. So, seeing how my friend who's standing there looks at me and says,
cues.zh: 她闭上眼睛张开嘴，那家伙绕过来，直接一坨奶油拍她脸上，你懂吧？我是说，这位女士惊呆了，毕竟是她的生日，打扮得漂漂亮亮的，结果直接被糊了一脸派，你知道吗？完全没有预警。我和朋友就站那儿看着，嘴巴张得老大，另一个朋友还在车里。然后站我旁边的朋友看着我，说：

cues.en: I think it might be Jack's birthday today. So we come in and we sit down. And I surreptitiously during the meal, get up and go and talk to the waiter. I'm like, hey, it's my friend's birthday today. I don't know if you do anything here. And he's like, oh, yeah, we got a thing we do. We'll come out. And so I was like, great. I go and sit back down. We're waiting. Eventually, they come out singing the song and everything. And our friend is looking a little bit bewildered.
cues.zh: 我觉得今天可能是Jack的生日。于是我们进去坐下。吃饭时我偷偷起身去找服务员，说：嘿，今天是我朋友的生日，不知道你们这儿有没有什么安排。他说：哦，有啊，我们有套流程，会出来的。我说太好了，回去坐下。我们等着，最后他们唱着歌什么的出来了。我们那位朋友看起来有点懵。

cues.en: And he later confessed that he thought that we had told them that it was his birthday so that we could get free cake or something like that. So he starts willingly playing along. And they put a little hat on him, and then, sure enough, they do the thing where they hold the little dab of whipped cream in front of him and closes his eyes. He opens his mouth, and the dude reaches around behind him, just slams him in the face. And I knew this was coming, so I had one of those disposable cameras that used to use a
cues.zh: 他后来承认，他以为是我们告诉店家那天是他生日，就为了蹭块免费蛋糕之类的。于是他开始心甘情愿地配合。他们给他戴了顶小帽子，然后果然，他们端着那一小坨奶油到他面前，他闭上眼睛张开嘴，那家伙从背后绕过来，直接糊他一脸。我知道这招要来，所以带了个那种一次性相机，以前用的那种

cues.en: back then you know and I had it under the tables already and so I got him right right at the moment you know just the look on his face is just pure shock all right anyway I hope that was more interesting than a three-minute you know description of my background okay let's talk about SSL on the future of authenticity and really this talk is about trust and
cues.zh: 那时候你懂的，我早就把它藏在桌子底下了，正好在那个瞬间拍到了他，他脸上那表情纯粹是震惊。好吧，希望这比听我花三分钟讲我的背景有意思。好，我们来聊聊SSL，关于真实性的未来，其实这个演讲讲的是信任，还有

cues.en: I want to start this talk out with another story. It's kind of a downer, but I feel like it's illustrative of the situation that we're in. And the story is about a company called Komodo. They're a certificate authority, and according to Netcraft, they certify somewhere between a quarter and a fifth of the certificates on the internet today. So they're the second largest certificate authority in the world. And in March of this year, they were hacked. The attacker was able to make off with a number of certificates.
cues.zh: 我想用另一个故事来开场。有点丧，但我觉得它能说明我们现在的处境。故事关于一家叫Komodo的公司。他们是证书颁发机构，根据Netcraft的数据，他们签发了当今互联网上四分之一到五分之一的证书。所以他们是全球第二大证书颁发机构。今年三月，他们被黑了。攻击者成功窃取了一批证书。

cues.en: Mail.google.com, login.yahoo.com, Skype. Basically everything that the attacker would need to intercept login credentials to all of the popular web mail providers and a few other services. And so immediately after the attack, the founder and CEO of Komodo issued a statement where he said, this attack was extremely sophisticated and critically executed. It was a very well orchestrated clinical attack.
cues.zh: Mail.google.com、login.yahoo.com、Skype。基本上，攻击者需要拦截所有流行网络邮件提供商以及其他一些服务的登录凭证，这些都在其中。攻击发生后，Komodo的创始人兼CEO立即发表声明，称这次攻击极其复杂且执行精准，是一场精心策划、冷静有序的攻击。

cues.en: and the attacker knew exactly what they needed to do and how fast they had to operate. He went on to add that all of the IP addresses involved in the attack were from Iran. You know what this means? Cyber. But he didn't leave it at any window. He actually spelled it out. He said, all of the above leads us to one conclusion, only that this was likely to be a state-driven attack. So he's painting a pretty complete picture for us here, right? This isn't just a hack. This is war.
cues.zh: 攻击者完全清楚自己需要做什么，以及必须以多快的速度操作。他接着补充说，所有参与攻击的IP地址都来自伊朗。你知道这意味着什么吗？网络攻击。但他并没有留下任何悬念，而是明确说了出来。他说，以上所有线索都指向一个结论，那就是这很可能是一场国家驱动的攻击。所以他为我们描绘了一幅相当完整的图景，对吧？这不仅仅是黑客攻击，这是战争。

cues.en: And who was to blame Komodo for falling into the full assaults of a state-sponsored invasion from a cyber army? And so ironically, it was these statements that really catapulted the story out of the trade press and into the mainstream media. And so a number of reporters called me, and they all had the same question. What does this mean? What can this attacker do? And I said, well, it means they can intercept communication to these websites. And the reporters would say, well, how? How would they use these certificates to do that?
cues.zh: 那么，Komodo陷入这场由国家支持的赛博军队全面入侵，该怪谁呢？讽刺的是，正是这些声明真正把这则故事从行业媒体推向了主流媒体。于是许多记者打电话给我，他们都有同一个问题：这意味着什么？这个攻击者能做什么？我说，这意味着他们可以拦截通往这些网站的通信。记者们会问，那怎么做到？他们如何利用这些证书来实现这一点？

cues.en: And I would say, well, you know, I think there's commercial solutions, you know, like the blue code and a few other, you know, kind of scary interception devices out there. And I was talking to one reporter who asked me, she said, no, what is the easiest way? What is the most straightforward way that an attacker would leverage these certificates? And I thought about it and I said, well, you know, the attacker could just use SSL sniff, which was a tool that I wrote to perform manual attacks against SSL connections. Now, interestingly enough,
cues.zh: 我会说，市面上其实有商业解决方案，比如 Blue Coat 以及其他一些挺吓人的拦截设备。当时我和一位记者聊，她问我：“不，攻击者利用这些证书最简单、最直接的方法是什么？”我想了想说：“攻击者其实可以直接用 SSLsniff”，这是我写的一个对 SSL 连接进行手动攻击的工具。更有趣的是，

cues.en: When Komodo published their incident report, they also published the IP address of the attacker, which is somewhat unusual. But I think that they were doing this to sort of underscore the Iran, Iran, Iran, Iran thing. Because the IP address is registered to a block in Iran. And so I was thinking about that reporter's question, SSL sniff and all that stuff. And so I thought, well, I wonder. And I looked at my web logs for my web server, where I host SSL sniff.
cues.zh: 当 Komodo 发布事件报告时，他们还公布了攻击者的 IP 地址，这其实挺少见的。但我觉得他们这样做是为了强调“伊朗、伊朗、伊朗、伊朗”这回事，因为那个 IP 属于伊朗的一个网段。于是我想起那位记者的提问，还有 SSLsniff 之类的东西。我想着：“嗯，会不会呢？”于是我查看了托管 SSLsniff 的 Web 服务器日志。

cues.en: And sure enough, the morning after the attack, the same IP address that Komodo had published downloaded SSL snap from my website. Now, there's some other interesting things in here. First of all, the attacker is running Windows. And also interestingly, the attacker's web browser is localized to US English. But the most interesting thing was the referrer. So I went back to my web logs and I found the point that the attacker initially made a connection with my website so that I could see
cues.zh: 果不其然，就在攻击发生后的第二天早上，Komodo 公布的那个 IP 地址从我的网站下载了 SSLsniff。这里面还有其他一些有意思的地方：首先，攻击者用的是 Windows；同样有趣的是，攻击者的浏览器语言是美式英语；但最耐人寻味的还是 Referrer。于是我回查了 Web 日志，找到了攻击者最初访问我网站的记录，想看看

cues.en: but the website that they had visited before. And so the referrer was a hack5 video on using SSL strip. For those of you who don't know, hack5 is sort of like a set of video tutorials that are pretty introductory material for people that are just getting interested in this kind of thing. So just to break this down for you, on one hand, we have the CEO of Komodo saying...
cues.zh: 他们之前访问了什么网站。结果 Referrer 居然是一期关于如何使用 SSLstrip 的 Hak5 视频。可能有人不知道，Hak5 就像是一系列视频教程，对刚对这类技术感兴趣的人来说是非常基础的入门资料。帮大家梳理一下：一方面，Komodo 的 CEO 声称……

cues.en: This is a clinical attack. And on the other hand, we see that the attacker is literally following video tutorials on the internet. I mean, maybe that was a great video. I don't know. I haven't watched it yet. It could have turned him into a clinical attacker. I'm not sure. And then there were a number of other embarrassing searches that led them to my same website again and again throughout the day. So I caught the Google search for furs, which were things like SSL, protocol, man in the middle, how-to, IP tables, pre-routing.
cues.zh: 一方面，这是一次外科手术般精准的攻击；但另一方面，我们却发现攻击者完全是在照着网上的视频教程一步步做。我的意思是，也许那视频真的很厉害，我不知道，我还没看过，说不定真能把他训练成顶尖黑客，我不确定。然后一整天下来，他们通过各种令人尴尬的搜索词一次又一次访问了我的网站。我抓到了来自 Google 搜索的来源记录，全是类似“SSL 协议”、“中间人攻击教程”、“iptables”、“PREROUTING”之类的词。

cues.en: Apparently he was having some trouble setting up their IP tables. So I was kind of chuckling about this to myself, you know, and then the attacker posted a communique. And it could not have been more embarrassing. I mean, he alternated between making these grandiose impossible claims about how he's hacked RSA and all this stuff, while simultaneously, very proudly declaring that he's capable of doing extremely trivial things like, you know, he can export functions from DLLs and create his own SOAP APIs and stuff like that.
cues.zh: 显然他在配置 iptables 时遇到了麻烦。我当时还暗自觉得好笑，结果接着攻击者就发了一份公报。那场面简直尴尬到了极点。我的意思是，他一边在那吹一些不可能做到的弥天大谎，比如他攻破了 RSA 之类的；一边又极其自豪地宣称自己能做些微不足道的小事，比如能从 DLL 里导出函数、能写自己的 SOAP API 等等。

cues.en: So this could not have been more embarrassing for really anybody involved. The attacker, Komodo. But what was worse is he just wouldn't shut up. He just kept posting communiques. Each one more embarrassing than the last. And I think he posted six in total. He also did interviews with the press and all this stuff. It was ridiculous. And so the Komodo CEO and founder responded to these events by making a statement where he said, if this were a secure and trusted DNS,
cues.zh: 对于所有卷入其中的人来说，这简直尴尬到无以复加，无论是攻击者还是 Komodo。但更糟的是，他就是闭不上嘴。他不停地发公报，一篇比一篇尴尬，我记得他总共发了六篇。他还接受了媒体采访等等，简直荒谬透顶。针对这些事件，Komodo 的 CEO 兼创始人发表了一份声明，他说：“如果有安全可信的 DNS，

cues.en: this issue would be a moot point, exclamation point. We need a secure and trusted DNS exclamation point. So this guy has just very enthusiastically declared that he does not understand the business that he's in. On one hand, he seems to be suggesting that DNS tampering is the only way to perform a man in the middle attack, which is just not true. And on the other hand, even if that were true, the reason that we have SSL certificates is to stop man in the middle attacks. If man in the middle attacks weren't possible,
cues.zh: 这个问题根本就不成立，感叹号！我们需要安全可信的 DNS，感叹号！”这位老兄就这么热情洋溢地向大家宣布：他根本不懂自己做的是什么业务。一方面，他似乎在暗示 DNS 篡改是发动中间人攻击的唯一途径，这根本不是事实。另一方面，退一步讲就算真是这样，我们之所以需要 SSL 证书，就是为了防范中间人攻击。如果中间人攻击不可能发生，

cues.en: we wouldn't need the certificates that he's selling us. Later that month, they got hacked two more times, and the next month they got hacked again. Now, you know, normally I wouldn't take this much time to be so critical of a company like Komodo, but I think it's an interesting story because I think there's an interesting question here, which is, what happened to Komodo? You know, after all of this, it couldn't have been more embarrassing, could not have been worse, really. You know, what happened to them? Nothing.
cues.zh: 我们也就根本不需要他卖给我们的证书了。当月晚些时候，他们又被黑了两次，下个月他们再次被黑。平时我通常不会花这么多时间去如此苛刻地批评像 Komodo 这样的公司，但我认为这是个有趣的故事，因为这里有一个值得玩味的问题：Komodo 后来怎么样了？经历这一切之后，局面尴尬到了极点，真是糟得不能再糟了。你们猜他们怎么着了？毫发无损，什么事都没发生。

cues.en: And their business didn't suffer. They didn't lose customers. They didn't get sued. Really, the only thing that happened to Komodo this year was the CEO was named entrepreneur of the year at the RSA conference. And so I think that this is the essence of the problem that we're looking at. This is the problem with SSL today. So let's take a moment and just sort of step back and look generally at secure protocols.
cues.zh: 他们的业务没有受到影响。他们没有失去客户。他们没有被告。实际上，今年Komodo唯一发生的事情就是CEO在RSA大会上被评为年度企业家。所以我认为这就是我们所面临问题的本质。这就是当今SSL的问题所在。让我们花点时间退后一步，从宏观角度审视安全协议。

cues.en: Any secure protocol needs to provide three things, secrecy, integrity, and authenticity. It has to provide all three. If one of these fails, the whole protocol will fall apart. But we need to remember that SSL, which is a secure protocol and it's trying to meet these objectives, was designed in the early 90s. And things were different there. There wasn't a lot of information available on how to design a secure protocol. Books like Applied Cryptography had not been published yet.
cues.zh: 任何安全协议都需要提供三点：保密性、完整性和真实性。它必须同时提供这三者。如果其中任何一个失效，整个协议就会崩溃。但我们需要记住，SSL作为一种旨在实现这些目标的安全协议，是在90年代初设计的。那时情况不同。关于如何设计安全协议的信息并不多。《应用密码学》这样的书还没有出版。

cues.en: If you wanted to use RSA the algorithm, you had to license the patent from RSA the company. You had to pay money in order to just even perform this type of cryptography. E-commerce didn't exist. The idea of transmitting your credit card number over the internet was totally foreign. There were no such things as web applications, really. People weren't really transmitting their login and password credentials through websites. And the internet itself was tiny.
cues.zh: 如果你想使用RSA算法，你必须从RSA公司获得专利许可。你仅仅为了执行这类密码学操作就得付钱。电子商务还不存在。通过互联网传输信用卡号的想法完全是天方夜谭。那时候根本没有Web应用这种东西。人们并不会通过网站传输登录凭据和密码。而且互联网本身规模很小。

cues.en: In 1994, according to ISC, there were less than 5 million hosts on the entire internet. Compare that to today, where we're about to run out of public-facing IP addresses at more than 4 billion, or at 4 billion. At the time, there are probably less than 10 secure sites that you could think of, less than 10 sites that, for some reason, you wanted traffic to be encrypted to these websites. Whereas today, there are more than 2 million certificates on the internet, more than 2 million sites that are using SSL.
cues.zh: 1994年，据 ISC 统计，整个互联网的主机还不到 500 万台。对比一下今天：面向公众的 IP 地址已经超过 40 亿个，我们眼看就要用完了，或者说，已经达到 40 亿个了。当时，你能想到的安全网站可能还不到 10 个，也就是说，出于某种原因，你希望与之通信的流量能加密的网站不到 10 个。而如今，互联网上的证书已超过 200 万个，使用 SSL 的网站也超过 200 万个。

cues.en: At the same time, it's worth remembering that SSL was developed at Netscape, and this was an environment of really intense pressure. The race was really on then, and this is the same place where a series of 4AM decisions gave us JavaScript. And we're still dealing with that today. So actually when you look at it, the designers of SSL were actually pretty heroic. They didn't have a lot to work with, and they were working in circumstances that are totally different than our circumstances today. And yet it served us pretty well.
cues.zh: 同时，值得记住的是，SSL 是在 Netscape 开发的，当时的环境压力非常大。那时竞争确实十分激烈，而 JavaScript 也是在同一个地方，由一系列凌晨 4 点做出的决定催生的。直到今天，我们还在承受这些决定的影响。所以，仔细想想，SSL 的设计者其实相当了不起。他们手头可用的资源不多，所处的环境也和我们今天截然不同。即便如此，SSL 还是很好地服务了我们。

cues.en: When it comes to these first two things, if you're seeing integrity, they did okay. There have been some problems, and there's still some problems, but the piece that has always caused some real friction is now causing real problems is the authenticity piece. Now, authenticity is important, of course, because normally if you establish a secure session with a website, the problem is that if you don't have authenticity, someone could have intercepted your connection to that website. They establish a secure session with you.
cues.zh: 说到前两项，如果你关注的是完整性，那它们做得还不错。虽然出现过一些问题，现在仍有一些问题，但一直以来真正造成摩擦、如今也带来实际麻烦的，是真实性这一部分。当然，真实性很重要，因为通常来说，如果你与某个网站建立了安全会话，但没有真实性验证，就可能有人拦截了你与该网站之间的连接。他们会和你建立一个安全会话。

cues.en: They make their own secure session with the website and just shuttle data back and forth, logging it in between. But what's easy to forget is that this attack, a man in the middle attack, was entirely theoretical in 94 or 95. The network tools didn't exist. This wasn't the kind of thing that was actively happening. This was thought of as an academic thing. It's like, oh, well, there's this other thing called the man in the middle attack. And we need to design something theoretically to prevent against that.
cues.zh: 他们与网站建立自己的安全会话，来回传输数据，并在中间记录。但容易忘记的是，这种攻击——中间人攻击——在94或95年完全是理论上的。网络工具还不存在。这不是那种正在实际发生的事情。这被视为学术问题。就像，哦，好吧，还有另一种叫中间人攻击的东西。我们需要在理论上设计一些东西来防止它。

cues.en: And so the designers came up with a solution that was certificates and certificate authorities, where every site has a certificate, and it's known to be authentic because it's assigned by a certificate authority, which is just some organization that we've decided to trust. So I had this hypothesis that we've outgrown the circumstances in which SSL was originally imagined, and that this is a different world today. And then I thought, well, I wonder if that's true. I wonder what they were actually thinking.
cues.zh: 于是设计者想出了一个解决方案，就是证书和证书颁发机构，每个网站都有证书，并且被认为是真实的，因为它是由证书颁发机构分配的，而证书颁发机构只是我们决定信任的某个组织。所以我有一个假设：我们已经超越了SSL最初设想的环境，今天是不同的世界。然后我想，好吧，我想知道那是否是真的。我想知道他们实际在想什么。

cues.en: And so I thought, well, I should talk to the people that designed SSL. And so I did some research, and I figured out that SSL was originally designed by this guy, Kip Hickman, who was a Netscape employee back in the day. And the last thing that Kip Hickman posted to the internet was in 1995. So it was difficult to find him. I talked to some people at Netscape who pointed me in the right direction, and eventually I tracked him down. And I basically just cold called him. And I talked to him on the phone, and he was a great guy.
cues.zh: 所以我想，好吧，我应该和设计SSL的人谈谈。于是我做了一些研究，发现SSL最初是由这个叫Kip Hickman的人设计的，他当时是Netscape的员工。而Kip Hickman最后发到互联网上的东西是在1995年。所以很难找到他。我和Netscape的一些人谈过，他们给我指了正确的方向，最终我找到了他。我基本上就是直接给他打了个冷电话。我在电话里和他交谈，他是个很棒的人。

cues.en: And he's like, oh, SSL. Yeah, I haven't thought about that in a long time. Wow, OK. And he's like, oh, yeah. And I was like, so what, certificate authorities, what's the deal? He's like, oh, that whole authenticity thing. He's like, yeah, we just threw that in at the end. He's like, SSL, it was never designed. We were designing it to prevent passive attacks, for the most part. We heard about this thing, the man in the middle attack. And so we just sort of threw that in at the end. He's like, really, that whole thing with certificates, it was a bit of a hand wave.
cues.zh: 他就说，哦，SSL。对，我已经很久没想过这个了。哇，好吧。然后他又说，哦，对。于是我问，那证书颁发机构呢，这到底是怎么回事？他说，哦，就是那个身份认证的事。他说，对，我们只是在最后把它加进去而已。他说，SSL 从来就不是这样设计的。我们设计它主要是为了防范被动攻击。我们听说过中间人攻击这种事。所以我们就在最后把身份认证大致加了进去。他说，说真的，证书那整套东西，其实有点含糊带过的意思。

cues.en: It's like, we didn't think it was going to work. We didn't know. And the idea back then, you could say, made sense. If you look at the number of domain names on the internet, back in 94, when that number, the graph, is approaching zero, it makes sense that, OK, maybe you have 10 sites that you could identify as secure sites. And so you have one organization that just looks at those 10 sites really carefully and makes a decision and signs those certificates.
cues.zh: 就好像我们当时也没觉得它能奏效。我们不知道。回头看，当时的想法其实是有道理的。如果看看互联网上的域名数量，在 1994 年，当图表上的这个数字还接近于零时，这种做法是说得通的：好吧，也许你能找出 10 个可以认定为安全网站的站点。于是由一个组织非常仔细地检查这 10 个站点，做出判断，然后为它们签发证书。

cues.en: But if you try and scale that up over time, to today when there's almost a billion domain names on the internet, and ideally we'd like all of them to be secure, it seems a little bit unrealistic to think, well, we're going to have an organization or even a set of organizations that's going to look appropriately closely at all of these domain names. When I asked Kip about how he saw the scaling over time, he was like, oh, scaling. We didn't really think about it. He was like, you've got to remember, at the time when this was designed, Yahoo
cues.zh: 但如果你试着随着时间推移扩展这套做法，到了今天，互联网上几乎有 10 亿个域名，而且理想情况下我们希望它们全都安全，那么认为我们会有一个组织，甚至一组组织，能够足够仔细地检查所有这些域名，似乎就有点不现实了。当我问 Kip 他怎么看待这种随时间推移而来的扩展问题时，他说，哦，扩展。我们当时确实没怎么想过。他说，你得记住，这套设计出来的时候，Yahoo

cues.en: was a web page with 30 links on it. I was like, that's what Yahoo was. I was like, oh, okay, yeah, that's different. And history has really borne this out. Ivan Ristic put together a nice little threat matrix of all of the possible problems with SSL that have cropped up in the past. And up over here in this corner, you see some of the problems with secrecy and integrity that have come up, but it's managed to sort of squeak by. And down here, there's some of the problems with user interaction. These are things like SSL strip.
cues.zh: 还只是一个上面有 30 个链接的网页。我说，Yahoo 当时就是这样。我说，哦，好吧，确实不一样。历史也确实证明了这一点。Ivan Ristic 整理了一份很不错的小型威胁矩阵，列出了过去出现过的所有 SSL 潜在问题。在这个角落里，你能看到一些已经出现过的保密性和完整性问题，但 SSL 还是勉强撑了过去。而在下面这里，还有一些与用户交互有关的问题，比如 SSL strip。

cues.en: But in terms of the protocol itself, this stuff up here with the authenticity piece has been where all the real problems are. And I think, you know, looking back at the Komodo thing, you know, the lesson from these events shouldn't be that this was cyber war, because I think pretty clearly it wasn't. But that this is happening every day. You know, that's the real story. You know, one of these domains the attacker got, login.live.com. I mean, you know, we should remember that Mike Zussman got this just by asking for it.
cues.zh: 但就协议本身而言，上面这些跟真实性有关的部分，才是所有真正问题所在。我觉得，回头看看 Komodo 那件事，这些事件给我们的教训不应该是“这是网络战”，因为很明显它不是。真正的教训是，这种事每天都在发生。这才是真正重点。比如其中一个被攻击者拿到的域名，login.live.com。我们得记住，Mike Zussman 只是开口要了一下就拿到了。

cues.en: You know, he didn't have to export functions from DLLs or Caritas and SOAP APIs or whatever, you know. He just sent in a request, you know. Eddy Nigg got Mozilla.com with no validation at all, just asked for it. VeriSign issued a code signing certificate for Microsoft Corporation to attackers that are still unidentified, you know, they were never discovered. I mean, this kind of thing happens all the time. Just recently, I needed to get an SSL certificate. So I went to this website, SSLinabox.com, you know, straight to the bottom of the barrel.
cues.zh: 他根本不需要从 DLL 里导出函数，也不用搞什么 Caritas 和 SOAP API 之类的。他就是发了个请求。Eddy Nigg 拿到 mozilla.com 也完全没有验证，就是要了一下。VeriSign 给微软公司签发了一张代码签名证书，对象却是至今身份不明的攻击者，他们从来没被查出来。这种事一直在发生。最近我需要弄一张 SSL 证书，就去了 SSLinabox.com 这个网站，直接找最底层的服务商。

cues.en: And it's one of these things where you have to create an account in order to submit anything. So I go to create the account, and when I click create, it just logged me into someone else's account. It's like the web app was broken. And I was like, well, fuck. I'm not even trying to hack this. I just want a certificate. So I logged out, and I tried to create an account, and it logged me into someone else's account. And every time I did it, I just got a different account.
cues.zh: 这种网站你得先注册账号才能提交任何东西。于是我去创建账号，点了一下创建，结果直接把我登录进了别人的账号。就像这个网页应用坏掉了一样。我当时就想，靠，我压根没想黑它，我只是想要张证书。于是我登出，再试着创建账号，结果又把我登进了另一个人的账号。每次我这么做，登进去的都是不同的账号。

cues.en: And the thing is, I didn't even bother emailing them about it, because I'm sure that they don't even care. There's this certificate authority that published the key to their certificate in the public directory of their web server. This is a certificate authority. And the thing is, you could kind of understand. I mean, not really, but you might be able to understand how it's possible that someone could have made this mistake. But it's still there.
cues.zh: 关键是，我甚至懒得发邮件告诉他们这件事，因为我确信他们根本不在乎。有一家证书颁发机构，居然把证书密钥发布在了他们Web服务器的公共目录里。这可是一家证书颁发机构啊。问题是，你大概也能理解——我是说，也不尽然，但你或许能理解怎么会有人犯这种错误。可它到现在还在那儿。

cues.en: You know, it's not like they like we're like, oh crap, you know and like removed it. It's since in 2009 The key to this certificate has been available for the public You know star com recently got hacked. We don't really know what happened and You know, you don't even have to hack anybody like if you've got the money you can just buy a certificate authority You can get a ca cert from geotrust. I think it's 50 grand Anybody has 50 grand to spend you're on ca cert intercept all the communication on the internet
cues.zh: 你知道，他们可没有像那样“哎呀糟糕”然后把它删掉。从2009年起，这个证书的密钥就一直对公众开放。你知道，star.com最近被黑了，我们其实也不太清楚发生了什么。而且，你甚至都不需要去黑任何人——只要有钱，你直接买一个证书颁发机构就行了。你可以从GeoTrust买一个CA证书，我记得是5万美元。只要谁有5万美元，你就能拿到CA证书，拦截互联网上的所有通信。

cues.en: I really like their iconography in the top right corner, because it really is. It's like, we're giving you the key to the world. They're not hiding anything. And what if this were a state-sponsored attack, this whole Komodo thing? I think it's worth realizing that the only reason that Iran would have to hack a certificate authority in order to issue certificates is because they don't have a certificate authority of their own.
cues.zh: 我真的很喜欢他们右上角的图标设计，因为确实很贴切，就像在说“我们把世界的钥匙交给你”。他们毫不遮掩。那如果这整个Komodo事件是国家支持的攻击呢？我觉得值得意识到的是，伊朗之所以要黑进一家证书颁发机构来签发证书，唯一的原因就是他们没有自己的证书颁发机构。

cues.en: Many other countries do. The EFF put together an excellent project called the SSL Observatory, where they scan the internet. And they put together a map of all the countries in the world that are currently capable of issuing certificates and thus intercepting secure communication. And it looks like this. I don't know if you can see, but way out in the middle of the Atlantic there, there's a little red speck. That's Bermuda. Bermuda can issue certificates. So I think the good news is that the vibe around the sort of
cues.zh: 很多其他国家也这样做。EFF 搞了一个非常棒的项目叫 SSL Observatory，他们会对互联网进行扫描。他们绘制了一张地图，列出了全球当前有能力签发证书、从而能够拦截安全通信的所有国家。它看起来就像这样。我不知道大家能不能看清，在茫茫的大西洋正中央，有一个小小的红色斑点。那是百慕大。百慕大可以签发证书。所以我觉得好消息是，这种事情的

cues.en: things seems to be shifting from the old vibe of total ripoff, which I think was just the general perception of certificate authorities, to the new vibe of total ripoff and mostly worthless. So there's been a lot of talk about moving forward and replacing certificate authorities with something else. But I think that if we're going to do that, it makes sense to really accurately identify the problem and figure out what it is that we're trying to solve so that we don't end up in the same situation again.
cues.zh: 氛围似乎正在发生转变，从以前那种“纯粹是坑人”的老氛围——我认为这只是大家对证书颁发机构的普遍看法——变成了“既坑人又基本上毫无价值”的新氛围。因此，有很多关于向前发展并用其他东西替代证书颁发机构的讨论。但我认为，如果我们打算这么做，首先弄清楚问题的真正所在、明确我们到底想解决什么问题就显得很有意义，这样我们就不会重蹈覆辙了。

cues.en: Now, there have been, I think, a few sort of general perceptions of what the problem might be. The first is people look at the EFF SSL Observatory data. So the EFF scan the internet and they put together a graph of all of the organizations in the world that are currently capable of signing certificates, and it's a lot of organizations. In fact, it's 650 different organizations are currently capable of intercepting communication.
cues.zh: 现在，我认为大家对问题可能出在哪里有一些普遍的看法。首先，人们会看 EFF 的 SSL Observatory 数据。EFF 对互联网进行了扫描，并绘制了一张图表，列出了全球当前有能力签署证书的所有组织，数量非常庞大。事实上，目前有 650 个不同的组织有能力拦截通信。

cues.en: And so I think one simplistic reaction to this is just to say, well, the problem is that there's too many certificate authorities. There's just too many of them. What we need is fewer certificate authorities. But I feel like this might be a little simplistic. For instance, remember when there was only one, and they could charge as much and do really whatever they wanted? And part of the problem here is really a scaling issue where we've gone from maybe 20 secure sites to 2 million secure sites, and ideally we'd like a billion secure sites.
cues.zh: 所以我觉得，对此一个过于简单的反应就是：问题在于证书颁发机构太多了，实在是太多了。我们需要的是更少的证书颁发机构。但我觉得这有点太简单了。比如，还记得当初只有一家的时候吗？他们想收多少钱就收多少钱，想干什么就干什么。这里的部分问题其实是规模问题：我们从大概20个安全网站发展到了200万个，而理想情况下我们想要10亿个安全网站。

cues.en: It seems like less is not really the answer. If anything, we would want more organizations that are capable of being on the ball here. Another kind of general perception is that there's just a few bad apples. That most of the certificate authorities are cool, and there's just a few certificate authorities that have given the whole thing a bad rap for everybody else. But I also don't know if this is true. I think that if you look closely, there's really nobody here that does not have dirt on their hands. Even VeriSign, back when they were the only game in town,
cues.zh: 看来“更少”并不是答案。如果说有什么的话，我们反而需要更多有能力在这件事上保持警觉的组织。另一种普遍看法是，这只是几颗老鼠屎坏了一锅粥。大多数证书颁发机构都没问题，只有少数几家给所有人抹了黑。但我也不确定这是不是真的。我觉得仔细看的话，这里其实没有谁的手是干净的。就连VeriSign，当年他们还是唯一选择的时候，

cues.en: At the same time that they had a business, issuing certificates and securing communication, had another section of their business where they were managing so-called lawful intercept services for governments. So the same organization that we had entrusted to secure our communication was also simultaneously making money by intercepting secure communication. And I think if you look closely, there's really nobody here that isn't similarly distressed. Another idea is that it's a scoping issue. That the problem is that
cues.zh: 在他们一边做生意、颁发证书、保障通信安全的同时，他们的另一块业务是在为政府管理所谓的合法拦截服务。也就是说，我们委托来保护我们通信的同一个组织，同时还在靠拦截安全通信赚钱。我觉得仔细看的话，这里真的没有谁不是同样一身问题。另一个想法是，这是范围问题。问题在于

cues.en: the authorities are all in the same scope. So, for instance, today, two authorities who can sign certificates and thus intercept secure communication on the internet are the Department of Homeland Security and the State of China. And so this idea, well, the problem is that the DHS can sign Chinese sites and China can sign U.S. sites. And really, if we just separated the scope and China could only sign sites in China and the Department of Homeland Security could only sign sites in the United States, everything would be cool.
cues.zh: 这些机构都在同一个范围内。比如今天，两个能签发证书、从而拦截互联网安全通信的机构，是美国国土安全部和中国。所以这个想法是：问题在于国土安全部能给中国网站签证书，中国也能给美国网站签证书。而如果我们真的把范围分开，中国只能给中国的网站签，国土安全部只能给美国的网站签，那一切就都没问题了。

cues.en: And while this might be an improvement, I feel like it's kind of a low bar. I think there are plenty of people in China that probably don't trust the state of China to certify sites even within their country. And likewise, I feel like there are plenty of people in the United States who don't trust the Department of Homeland Security to be certifying their communication either. So in order to answer this question, what is the problem, I think it's a good idea to look back at the first question. What happened to Komodo? Well, nothing happened to Komodo.
cues.zh: 虽然这可能是一种改进，但我觉得这标准未免太低了。我觉得中国有很多人可能并不信任中国政府来认证他们国内的网站。同样，我觉得美国也有很多人不信任国土安全部来认证他们的通信。因此，为了回答“问题究竟是什么”这个问题，我觉得最好回顾一下第一个问题：Komodo 怎么了？其实，Komodo 什么事也没有。

cues.en: But why? Why did nothing happen? What could we have done? If I decide that I don't trust Komodo, and I don't, the very best thing that I can do is remove them from the trust database in my web browser. I could say, OK, they are no longer a trusted authority. The problem is that if I do that, somewhere between a quarter and a fifth of the internet just disappears. Totally breaks. I can't visit those sites anymore.
cues.zh: 但为什么呢？为什么什么事都没发生？我们本可以做什么？如果我决定不信任 Komodo，而我的确不信任，我能做的最好的事就是把它从我网页浏览器的信任数据库中移除。我可以说，好吧，它们不再是受信任的机构。问题是，如果我这么做了，互联网上有四分之一到五分之一的内容就会直接消失。彻底崩溃。我再也访问不了那些网站了。

cues.en: And sure, I could take an ideological stance to never visit those sites again because they're mixed up in the Komodo cabal of whatever. But really, there's no appropriate response. And the thing to remember is that this is as true for browser vendors as it is for you or me. A browser vendor cannot remove Komodo from their trust database because they're just going to be breaking somewhere between a quarter and a fifth of the internet for all of their users. They're in the exact same situation that you and I are.
cues.zh: 当然，我可以采取一种意识形态立场，再也不去访问那些网站，因为它们和 Komodo 的什么阴谋勾结在一起。但说实话，根本没有合适的应对办法。需要记住的是，这对浏览器厂商来说，和你或我是一样的。浏览器厂商无法将 Komodo 从其信任数据库中移除，因为这会给他们的所有用户导致互联网四分之一到五分之一的崩溃。他们的处境和你我一模一样。

cues.en: The truth is that somewhere along the line, we made a decision to trust Komodo. And now we are locked into trusting them forever. And I think that this is the essence of what we're looking at today. That we can void on all the problems that we've had with certificate authorities to a single missing property. And I call this property trust agility. The idea is that trust agility provides two things. One,
cues.zh: 事实是，在某个环节，我们决定信任 Komodo。现在我们就被永久锁死在对它的信任里。我认为这就是我们今天所面对问题的本质：我们可以把所有证书颁发机构的问题，归结到一个缺失的属性上。我称这个属性为“信任敏捷性”。这个理念是，信任敏捷性提供两件事。第一，

cues.en: that a trust decision can be easily revised at any time. There are plenty of people that say, oh, Moxie, you don't trust anybody. That's not true. I mean, there are plenty of organizations that I could identify today that I trust to secure my communication, for me. But what seems insane is to think that I could identify an organization or set of organizations that I would be willing to trust not just now, but forever.
cues.zh: 信任决策可以在任何时候被轻松修订。有很多人说，哦，Moxie，你谁都不信任。那不是真的。我的意思是，今天我能找出很多组织，我愿意信任它们来为我保障通信安全。但真正疯狂的是，认为我能找出一个或一组组织，不仅现在愿意信任，而且永远愿意信任。

cues.en: regardless of whether they continue to warrant my trust and without any incentive to continue behaving in a trustworthy way. The second property of trust agility is that individual users can decide where to anchor their trust. And this could be the same thing as saying individual browsers can decide where to anchor their trust. And I think this is important. Right now, there's this idea, oh, there's this scoping problem. You know that VeriSign and Komodo are in the same scope. And that, well, if we just separated the scopes, then if VeriSign did something particularly egregious,
cues.zh: 不管它们是否继续值得我的信任，也不管它们是否有任何激励去继续保持可信行为。信任敏捷性的第二个属性是，单个用户可以决定把自己的信任锚定在哪里。这也可以等同于说，单个浏览器可以决定把自己的信任锚定在哪里。我认为这很重要。现在有一种想法，哦，存在作用域问题。你知道 VeriSign 和 Komodo 在同一个作用域里。那么，如果我们只是把作用域分开，那么如果 VeriSign 做了特别恶劣的事，

cues.en: A site like Facebook could switch to a different certificate authority and this would actually have some significance because VeriSign would be unable to continue signing certificates for Facebook, which is currently not the case. But I think if it's been a struggle to get websites to deploy HTTPS or SSL to begin with, it seems a little bit far-fetched to think that they're going to continue making really active decisions in our best interests.
cues.zh: 像 Facebook 这样的网站就可以切换到另一个证书颁发机构，这实际上会有一些意义，因为 VeriSign 将无法继续为 Facebook 签发证书，而目前情况并非如此。但我认为，如果一开始就让网站部署 HTTPS 或 SSL 都很费劲，那么认为它们会继续做出真正积极的、符合我们最佳利益的决策，就有点牵强了。

cues.en: And what's worse in this increasingly globalized world, it doesn't seem like it's really possible to make one trust decision for everybody. Different people live in different contexts with different threats and have different needs and probably trust different individuals. And so what's more, it's our data. It's our data that's at risk here, not the site administrator, not the company that's operating this web service. It's the user's data. And I feel like it should be the user's
cues.zh: 而在如今这个日益全球化的世界里，更糟糕的是，似乎根本不可能为所有人做出统一的信任决策。不同的人生活在不同的环境中，面临不同的威胁，有着不同的需求，信任的对象可能也各不相同。更重要的是，这是我们自己的数据。真正面临风险的是我们的数据，而不是网站管理员，也不是运营该 Web 服务的公司。这是用户的数据。我觉得应该由用户……

cues.en: or the browsers who get to decide who to trust. This property, the individual users decide where they can anchor their trust is really just a simple but powerful inversion of the way that things already work. Currently, there's three entities involved in any one of these transactions. There's the client, the server, and the authority. And this trust relationship is initiated by the server. The server talks to an authority and says, hey, please certify me. The authority responds with a certificate that is eventually
cues.zh: ……或者由浏览器来决定信任谁。让每个用户自行决定把信任锚定在哪里，这种机制其实只是对现有运作方式的一次简单却强大的反转。目前，任何此类交互都涉及三个实体：客户端、服务器和认证机构。而这种信任关系是由服务器发起的。服务器联系认证机构说：“嘿，请给我颁发证书。”机构随后返回证书，并最终……

cues.en: given back to the user through the site. And what we're talking about here is just doing a simple inversion, where it's the user or the client that initiates this trust transaction and talks to the authority, the authority, and says, please certify the site for me. The authority certifies that site and responds back to the user. The reason this is so powerful is because now this means the user can decide what authority they need to talk to, which means that this issue of scoping is not such a big deal. The fact that the Department of Homeland Security can sign sites
cues.zh: ……通过网站提供给用户。而我们在这里讨论的只是一次简单的反转：由用户或客户端发起这种信任交互，主动联系认证机构说：“请帮我验证这个网站。”机构对该网站进行认证后返回给用户。这种方式之所以如此强大，是因为用户现在可以自行决定联系哪家认证机构，这意味着管辖权限的问题就不再是什么大问题了。哪怕美国国土安全部可以为……

cues.en: in China, it's not an issue because users in China will just ignore it and talk to some Chinese authority. Or they might decide they don't trust China either, and they talk to some NGO or something else instead. I think that these two components of trust agility are really powerful, and I think that they are exactly what's missing from the CA system today, and that is where all our problems have come from. So I want to take a few minutes to talk about DNSSEC.
cues.zh: ……中国的网站签名，这也完全不是问题，因为中国的用户可以直接忽略它，转而去联系中国的认证机构。或者他们可能觉得中国机构也不可信，转而去联系某个 NGO 之类的其他机构。我认为信任敏捷性的这两个要素非常强大，这也正是当今 CA 体系所缺失的，而这正是我们所有问题的根源。所以我想花几分钟来谈谈 DNSSEC。

cues.en: because there's been a little bit of talk recently about using DNSSEC to replace the authenticity piece of SSL. And the basic idea is this. You take your SSL certificate on your site and you shove it in your DNS record. That's basically the gist of it. So you have a cert, you put in your DNS record. That way, when a client goes to contact a site, it does a DNS lookup, it gets back a DNS response with not only the IP address, but also the server certificate embedded in the DNS response.
cues.zh: 因为最近有些讨论，说用 DNSSEC 来替代 SSL 中负责真实性验证的部分。基本思路是这样：你把自己网站上的 SSL 证书塞进 DNS 记录里，差不多就是这么回事。也就是你有证书，把它放进 DNS 记录。这样，客户端去联系一个网站时，会做一次 DNS 查询，拿回的 DNS 响应里不仅有 IP 地址，还内嵌了服务器证书。

cues.en: That way, when they connect to the server, they just make sure that the certificate they see is the same thing they got in the DNS response. And this thing is known to be authentic because it's signed because we're using DNSSEC. Now, this scheme has a really immediately kind of visceral appeal. And I think it's because people tend to mentally associate DNS with the word distributed. And distributed sounds really good right now. You know, it sounds like exactly what we need. After suffering under the centralized yoke of certificate authorities for all these years,
cues.zh: 这样，它们连接服务器时，只要确认自己看到的证书和 DNS 响应里拿到的是同一个东西。而这个东西之所以被认为是真实的，是因为它被签名了，因为我们用了 DNSSEC。这个方案有一种很直接、直击本能的吸引力。我觉得这是因为人们容易在心理上把 DNS 和“分布式”这个词联系起来。而“分布式”现在听起来非常棒。你知道，听起来正是我们需要的。毕竟这些年在证书颁发机构的中心化枷锁下受了这么多苦，

cues.en: It would feel good to just wipe them off the page and replace them with a distributed system instead. But when you start to look closely at it, the way that DNS works and DNS set works is that it's the information that is distributed. The information in the DNS records is distributed across the various zones on the internet. But the trust is incredibly centralized and hierarchical. And this is actually exactly how the CA system works today. The information, the certificates, are distributed across the web servers of the sites
cues.zh: 把它们彻底抹掉、换成一个分布式系统，会让人感觉很爽。但当你仔细看时，DNS 和 DNSSEC 的运作方式是：被分布式的是信息。DNS 记录里的信息分布在整个互联网的各个区域中。但信任却极其中心化、层级化。而这其实正是今天 CA 系统的运作方式。信息，也就是证书，分布在互联网上提供服务的各个网站的 Web 服务器上，

cues.en: that are serving them on the internet, and the trust is highly centralized in this hierarchy of certificate authorities. So the next question is, well, OK, if it's still centralized trust, maybe there's something about the people that we have to trust, or maybe there's some increased trust agility here that would be appealing. So let's look at the trust requirements. There are three main classes of people that you have to trust under DNSSEC. The first is the registrars. I feel like if CAs are sketchy,
cues.zh: 也就是在互联网上提供这些证书的服务器上，而信任则高度集中在证书颁发机构的层级体系中。那么下一个问题是，好吧，如果信任仍然是中心化的，也许我们要信任的人有些特别之处，或者这里也许有一些更高的信任敏捷性会很有吸引力。那我们就看看信任要求。在 DNSSEC 下，你主要必须信任三类主体。第一类是注册商。我觉得如果 CA 已经够可疑了，

cues.en: These people are, they're taking it up a notch. Personally, I think it should be laughable that the current first step in deploying DNSSEC is to create an account with GoDaddy. I think that should be laughable. The second class of people that we have to trust here are the TLDs. So these are the companies that manage the top-level domains. So in the case of .com and .net, the largest TLDs on the internet, the company that manages those is VeriSign.
cues.zh: 那这些人更是有过之而无不及。我个人认为，部署 DNSSEC 当前的第一步竟然是去 GoDaddy 开个账户，这应该很可笑。我觉得这应该很可笑。这里我们必须信任的第二类主体是 TLD，也就是管理顶级域名的公司。比如 .com 和 .net 是互联网上最大的 TLD，管理它们的公司就是 VeriSign。

cues.en: Same player, same game. If you look at other TLDs like .org and .edu, the companies that manage them are probably not companies that you've ever heard of. I would at least suggest that if you were to think, oh, who's like a really trustworthy company? Who's really, you know, has a strong sense of integrity, these companies are probably not the first that would come to mind.
cues.zh: 换汤不换药。看看像 .org 和 .edu 这样的其他 TLD，管理它们的公司你可能听都没听过。我至少敢说，如果你去想“哪家公司真正值得信赖？谁真正极具信誉”，这些公司大概绝不会是你最先想到的。

cues.en: You know, take a minute to look at the organizations that manage the other TLDs and look at the executive boards, look at the people managing the operations, and ask yourself, are these the people that I want to trust with all of my secure communication in the future? There's also the country code top-level domains. So does everyone that's using TLDs that are kind of hip, like .io, .cc, and .ly, trust the corresponding governments for these countries to secure all of their communication?
cues.zh: 不妨花点时间看看管理其他 TLD 的机构，看看它们的董事会，看看负责实际运营的人，然后问问自己：未来我所有的安全通信，真的要托付给这些人吗？此外还有国家代码顶级域名。那些在使用 .io、.cc、.ly 这类挺时髦的 TLD 的人，难道真的信任对应国家的政府能保障他们所有的通信安全吗？

cues.en: What about TLDs like .irn.cn? Should the citizens of these countries have to trust their governments with all of their secure communication to local sites? This is the current picture of what countries around the world are capable of intercepting secure communication based on the EFF SSL Observatory data. This is what that picture would look like under DNS. And if the recent domain seizures are any indication of the future, it seems like these TLDs could be dangerous.
cues.zh: 像 .ir、.cn 这样的 TLD 又如何呢？这些国家的公民难道就必须把访问本地网站的所有安全通信，都托付给当地政府吗？根据 EFF SSL Observatory 的数据，这是目前全球各国拦截安全通信能力的现状图。而如果放在 DNS 体系下，这张图就会变成这样。如果最近的域名扣押事件预示了未来的走向，那么这些 TLD 看起来可能会非常危险。

cues.en: And then the third class of people that we have to trust here is The Root, and that's ICANN. Now, I don't have any particular beef with ICANN, but while ICANN has made a great effort to be a sort of global organization, as far as I know, and I could be wrong, but as far as I know, fundamentally, they are just a California 501c3 nonprofit, which as far as I know means that they have to abide by laws in the United States.
cues.zh:
接着我们需要信任的第三类主体就是根区，也就是 ICANN。
@@
现在，我对 ICANN 并没有什么特别的意见，但虽然 ICANN 已经付出巨大努力去成为一个某种意义上的全球化组织，据我所知，我可能搞错了，但据我所知，从根本上讲，他们只是一家加州的 501(c)(3) 非营利组织，据我所知，这意味着他们必须遵守美国的法律。

cues.en: legislation that's been coming up recently like COICA and protect IP and this kind of thing. You know, to me the real lesson here isn't whether this passes or not because there's been some kind of heroic efforts to prevent this legislation from going through. But I think the thing to take away from this is that they're trying to pass legislation that messes with this stuff and maybe one day they'll succeed. And I think ICANN would be subject to that regulation in that case. The worst part about
cues.zh: 最近出台的一些立法，比如COICA和保护IP之类的。对我来说，真正的教训不在于这些法案是否通过，因为已经有一些英勇的努力在阻止这些立法通过。但我认为从中应该吸取的是，他们正试图通过干扰这些事情的立法，也许有一天他们会成功。我认为在那种情况下，ICANN将受制于那项法规。最糟糕的部分是

cues.en: all of these organizations is that this system actually provides reduced trust agility. That today, even as unrealistic as it might be, I could still choose to remove VeriSign from my list of trusted certificate authorities. But there is nothing that I can do to stop VeriSign from being the company that manages the .com and .net TLBs. So if we sign up to trust these people, we're signing up not to trust them just now, but forever.
cues.zh: 所有这些组织共同的问题是，这套系统实际上降低了信任灵活性。今天，尽管可能不太现实，我仍然可以选择把VeriSign从我的受信任证书颁发机构列表中移除。但我却无法阻止VeriSign成为管理.com和.net顶级域的公司。所以，如果我们选择信任这些人，我们承诺的不只是现在信任他们，而是永远信任他们。

cues.en: regardless of whether they should continue to warn our trust, with no ability to change our mind about whether we should continue trusting them, without any incentives to continue behaving appropriately. So, let's talk about things that I'm a little bit more inspired by. There's a project called Perspectives, which came out of Carnegie Mellon University, and it was done by Dan Winland, David Anderson, and Adrian Perick. And it was originally a paper that was published on using multipath probing in order to provide authenticity.
cues.zh: 不管它们是否还值得我们信任，我们都没有办法改变是否继续信任它们的决定，而且它们也没有任何继续保持合规行为的动力。所以，让我们来聊聊一些更让我受启发的事情。有一个名叫 Perspectives 的项目，来自卡耐基梅隆大学，由 Dan Winland、David Anderson 和 Adrian Perick 完成。它最初是一篇关于利用多路径探测来提供真实性验证的论文。

cues.en: for SSH and SSL. And the concept is fundamentally about perspective. The basic idea is this. You connect to a secure site, you get back a certificate, and you think, wow, I wonder if this certificate is good or not. How do I validate it? Well, what you do is you contact an authority, then you say, hey, what certificate do you see for PayPal.com in this case? The authority makes its own connection to the website, gets its own certificate back, just like a normal web browser would.
cues.zh: 针对 SSH 和 SSL。这个概念从根本上讲就是关于视角。基本思路是这样的。你连接到一个安全网站，拿到一个证书，然后你会想，哇，不知道这个证书到底好不好。我该怎么验证它呢？好吧，你的做法是联系一个权威机构，然后问，嘿，在这种情况下，你看到的 PayPal.com 的证书是什么？权威机构自己连接到该网站，拿回它自己的证书，就像普通网页浏览器那样。

cues.en: And then sends that certificate back to you as the client. Now, you compare the thing you got from the authority with the thing you got from the site, and you make sure that they're the same. And so what you're essentially doing is you're using some network perspective to get a different view on the same site, that you have a different network path from wherever the authority is communicating from. And we call these authorities notaries. And you don't have to talk to just one notary. You can talk to any number of notaries.
cues.zh: 然后把那个证书作为客户端发回给你。现在，你把从权威机构拿到东西和从网站拿到东西进行比对，确保它们是一样的。所以你本质上在做的是，利用某种网络视角来获取对同一个网站的不同视图，你所使用的网络路径与权威机构进行通信的路径不同。我们把这些权威机构称为公证人。而且你不一定非得和一个公证人通信。你可以和任意数量的公证人通信。

cues.en: and they can be distributed around the world so they each have their own unique network path to the same destination. You're essentially building a constellation of trust. This idea of using perspective is actually not new. It's how SSL works right now. Right now, if a site administrator wants to get a certificate for its site, what does the administrator do? They contact an authority and they say, hey, could you please issue a certificate for my site? And what does the authority do?
cues.zh: 它们可以分布在世界各地，因此每个节点到同一个目的地都有自己独特的网络路径。你本质上是在构建一个信任星座。这种利用视角的想法其实并不新鲜。现在的 SSL 就是这样工作的。现在，如果一个网站管理员想要为其站点获取证书，管理员会怎么做？他们会联系一个权威机构并说，嘿，能请为我的站点颁发一个证书吗？权威机构会怎么做？

cues.en: they send an email to the site with a verification code in it. And if the administrator can receive the verification code and send it back to the authority, the authority issues the certificate. So it's just using another form of network perspective to do the same thing. We're just trying to invert this relationship. So instead of being site-initiated, it's user-initiated. Now, perspectives, when it was released, came with an implementation.
cues.zh: 它们会向该网站发送一封包含验证码的电子邮件。如果管理员能够收到验证码并将其发回给权威机构，权威机构就会颁发证书。所以这只是利用另一种形式的网络视角来做同样的事情。我们只是试图颠倒这种关系。因此，它不再由网站发起，而是由用户发起。现在，Perspectives 在发布时自带了一个实现。

cues.en: But the implementation was kind of limited. It was initially designed for self-signed certificates, and so it has had some challenges. The first big challenge is completeness. Since it was initially designed for self-signed certificates, it only works for the initial connection on the your web browser sends. So it doesn't work for any of the background content, the images, CSS, JavaScript, all that stuff. So it's not possible to really eliminate certificate authorities completely using perspectives.
cues.zh: 但这个实现有点局限。它最初是为自签名证书设计的，因此遇到了一些挑战。第一个大挑战是完整性。由于它最初是为自签名证书设计的，它只适用于你的网页浏览器发送的初始连接。因此，它不适用于任何背景内容，比如图片、CSS、JavaScript 以及所有这些东西。所以，要完全消灭证书权威机构，只靠 Perspectives 是不可能做到的。

cues.en: The second problem was privacy. If every time I make a secret connection to a website, I have to make another connection to a notary. I'm now leaking my entire connection history to the notary, and that seems a little bit unfortunate. And the last problem is responsiveness. Prospective suffered from this idea of notary lag. What would happen is you get a certificate, you contact a notary, and you say, hey, what do you see for paypal.com? And the notary would make a connection to paypal.com and see a certificate.
cues.zh: 第二个问题是隐私。如果我每次与网站建立秘密连接时，都得再联系一个公证人，那我就把自己的整个连接历史都泄露给了公证人，这似乎有点不太妙。最后一个问题是响应速度。Prospective 就受困于这种公证人延迟。情况是这样的：你拿到一个证书，联系公证人，问，嘿，你看到的 paypal.com 是什么情况？然后公证人会去连接 paypal.com，看到一份证书。

cues.en: The problem is the notary would cache the response so that it wasn't constantly having to connect out to all of these sites, and then just periodically at some interval pull the site, like once a day or something like that, all the sites that it had certificates for in order to see whether the site had switched to a different certificate. The problem is that if a site did switch to a different certificate, your responses from the notary would be invalid for the duration of the pull interval.
cues.zh: 问题在于，公证人会缓存响应，这样它就不必不停地去连接所有这些站点，而是每隔一段时间——比如每天一次——去拉取它持有证书的所有站点，看看站点是否换成了不同的证书。问题在于，如果某个站点确实换了证书，那么在拉取间隔期间，你从公证人那里得到的响应就是无效的。

cues.en: So what I've done is I've taken this concept of using perspective, and I've built on it to create a system that I call convergence. Convergence is a new protocol, a new client implementation, and a new server implementation of this concept. The first thing that we do is try and address the perspective challenges. We eliminate notary lag by basically when you contact the notary, you also send what you saw. So now the notary doesn't have to do any polling.
cues.zh: 所以我所做的是，采纳了使用透视这个概念，并在此基础上构建了一个我称之为 convergence 的系统。Convergence 是这个概念的一套新协议、一个新客户端实现和一个新服务器实现。我们做的第一件事是尝试解决透视带来的挑战。我们通过这样一种方式消除公证人延迟：当你联系公证人时，你也把自己看到的内容发过去。这样公证人就不必再做任何轮询了。

cues.en: It just has to contact the server in the case of the cache miss or cache mismatch. There's no more notary lag. The next thing that we did was add privacy. So this is two parts. The first part was through local caching. So now whenever you contact a notary and you say, hey, what do you think of the certificate? If it says, hey, this is A-OK, you go ahead and cache that certificate locally. That way the next time you connect to the site, you get the same certificate back. All you have to do is check the local cache and say, yeah, this thing is good. And you don't even have to talk to a notary.
cues.zh: 它只需要在缓存未命中或缓存不匹配时联系服务器。不再有公证延迟了。接下来我们做的是添加隐私保护。这分为两部分。第一部分是通过本地缓存实现的。现在，每当你联系公证人并询问“嘿，你觉得这个证书怎么样？”如果它说“嘿，这完全没问题”，你就把该证书缓存在本地。这样下次你连接到该网站时，你会拿回同样的证书。你只需检查本地缓存并确认“对，这东西没问题”，甚至不需要联系公证人。

cues.en: So now you're only leaking your connection history the first time you visit a secure site or whenever the secure site's certificate changes. But so that still doesn't seem that great. So the next thing we do is implement notary bouncing. The idea is that you have a set of notaries that you have configured as notaries that you trust, and you want to talk to all of them. And the first thing that you do is randomly select one of the notaries and assign it as a bounce.
cues.zh: 所以现在你只在首次访问安全网站或安全网站证书变更时才会泄露连接历史。但这看起来仍然不够好。所以我们接下来实现的是公证人中继。思路是你有一组配置为可信公证人的公证人，你想与它们全部通信。你做的第一件事是随机选择其中一个公证人，将其指定为中继。

cues.en: And you connect to that notary, and then you tunnel SSL through the notary to all the notaries that you want to talk to. So the bounce notary is just a dumb proxy, shoveling bytes around. And it doesn't have any visibility into what you're querying about. The notaries that you're talking to know what you're asking about, but they don't know who you are. And the bounce notary knows who you are, but it doesn't know who you're asking about. These SSL connections to the destination notaries are done using
cues.zh: 你连接到该公证人，然后通过该公证人将 SSL 隧道打通到你想要通信的所有公证人。因此中继公证人只是一个笨代理，搬运字节而已。它无法看到你在查询什么。你通信的公证人知道你在问什么，但不知道你是谁。中继公证人知道你是谁，但不知道你在问什么。这些到目标公证人的 SSL 连接是使用

cues.en: static pre-shared keys that are configured whenever you add the notary to begin with in your browser, just like with certificate authorities now. Convergence is a Firefox add-on, and it looks exactly like the normal Firefox experience. The only difference is in the upper right-hand corner, you get this little convergence button. If you click this button and enable convergence, you are completely divorced from the CA system. Everything, foreground content, background content,
cues.zh: 静态预共享密钥完成的，这些密钥在你最初将公证人添加到浏览器时配置，就像现在的证书颁发机构一样。Convergence 是一个 Firefox 附加组件，外观与正常的 Firefox 体验完全一样。唯一的区别是在右上角，你会看到这个小 Convergence 按钮。如果你点击此按钮并启用 Convergence，你就完全脱离了 CA 系统。一切内容，前台内容、后台内容，

cues.en: the certificate authority certificates in your web browser are completely ignored. Everything looks exactly the same. The only difference is that normally if you visit a secure site and you put your mouse over the favicon, you'll see a little tool tip about who has certified this communication. The only difference with convergence is we are taking the certificate authorities completely out of the picture. Everything else works the same.
cues.zh: 你 Web 浏览器中的证书颁发机构证书都被完全忽略。一切看起来完全一样。唯一的区别是，通常如果你访问一个安全网站并将鼠标悬停在网站图标上，你会看到一个小提示，说明谁认证了此通信。Convergence 的唯一区别是我们将证书颁发机构完全排除在外。其他一切工作方式相同。

cues.en: The notary implementation is available free, open source. Anybody can run their own notary. It requires very little resources, and it's designed to be extensible. The protocol is a REST protocol, and the idea is to design a protocol that supported a number of different backends. So by default, the default backend for the notary is to use network perspective. But you could write any number of other backends for the notary. For instance, if you like TNSEC,
cues.zh: 公证人（notary）的实现是免费且开源的。任何人都可以运行自己的公证人服务。它对资源的需求极低，并且采用了可扩展的设计。该协议是一个 REST 协议，其设计理念是支持多种不同的后端。因此默认情况下，公证人的默认后端使用的是网络视角（network perspective）。但你完全可以为公证人编写任意数量的其他后端。例如，如果你喜欢 TNSEC，

cues.en: The notary could do DNSSEC to validate the certificate on the back end. It wouldn't have to use network perspective. If you're crazy, it could use CA signatures to validate certificates. You could even use notaries as fraud ends to other services, like a notary front end to the EFF's SSL Observatory, which the EFF has volunteered to run. And you can configure notaries that do different things. So you could have a set of trusted notaries. Each one does a different thing.
cues.zh: 公证人可以使用 DNSSEC 在后端验证证书。它不必非得使用网络视角。如果你觉得疯狂，它甚至可以使用 CA 签名来验证证书。你甚至可以将公证人用作其他服务的前端，比如作为 EFF 的 SSL Observatory 的公证人前端，而 EFF 已经自愿运行该服务。你可以配置执行不同任务的公证人。因此，你可以拥有一组受信任的公证人，每个公证人执行不同的任务。

cues.en: Convergence implementation also has a threshold that you can set on what percentage of the notaries have to agree in order for things to be secure. I think the default is consensus. So what this means is that in the current CAA system, you have some number of certificate authorities, and if one of them is a bad actor, you're completely out of luck. And we're inverting that here, where the more
cues.zh: Convergence 的实现还提供了一个阈值设置，你可以设定必须有多少比例的公证人达成一致，才能确保安全性。我想默认值是达成共识。这意味着在当前的 CA 系统中，你有一定数量的证书颁发机构，如果其中一个作恶，你就彻底完蛋了。而在这里我们将其颠倒了过来，你拥有的

cues.en: authorities that you have, the more notaries that you configure, the better off you are because it means that all of them have to be in cahoots to misbehave and intercept your SSL communication. And we have full trust agility. If we decide we don't like one of these people, we can just remove it, and there are no implications. Everything continues to work exactly as it normally would. Nothing breaks. And if you like, you could replace it with a different one that does the same thing because you think that they're more trustworthy. Other nice things here are that the servers do nothing.
cues.zh: 权威机构越多，配置的公证人越多，你的处境就越安全，因为这意味着必须所有公证人都串通起来作恶，才能拦截你的 SSL 通信。我们拥有完全的信任灵活性。如果我们决定不再信任其中某个机构，直接将其移除即可，不会产生任何影响。一切都会像往常一样正常运转，不会出现任何故障。如果你愿意，可以用另一个执行相同任务的机构替换它，因为你觉得后者更值得信赖。这里另一个极好的特性是，服务器什么都不用做。

cues.en: people's web servers, you don't have to make any changes, which means we don't have to migrate the internet to anything else. All we have to do is implement convergence in the four major browsers and be done. That would be it. That would be the end of the CA system right there. We don't have to make any changes across the internet anywhere else. Other nice things, you don't get any more self-signed certificate warnings. The concept of a self-signed certificate does not exist in the convergent system. Certificates are certificates. That's it. There are a few problems.
cues.zh: 人们的Web服务器，你无需做任何更改，这意味着我们不必将互联网迁移到其他任何东西上。我们所需要做的只是在四大浏览器中实现收敛，就大功告成了。就是这样。那将是CA系统的终结。我们不需要在互联网上的其他地方做任何改变。还有其他的好处，你不会再收到自签名证书的警告了。在收敛系统中不存在自签名证书的概念。证书就是证书。仅此而已。但有几个问题。

cues.en: The first is the Citibank problem, what's known as the Citibank problem. Right now, if you're running convergence and you visit Citibank.com, you will get a certificate warning, an untrusted certificate warning. And the problem is that Citibank apparently has a couple of hundred different SSL certificates. And each one is on a different SSL accelerator.
cues.zh: 首先是花旗银行问题，也就是众所周知的“花旗银行问题”。现在，如果你正在运行收敛，并访问Citibank.com，你会收到一个证书警告，一个不受信任的证书警告。问题在于，花旗银行显然有几百个不同的SSL证书，每个都部署在不同的SSL加速器上。

cues.en: So every time you connect, you get a different certificate, which means that all of the notaries see different certificates, your browser sees a different certificate, and it looks identical to the case of being attacked. The good news is that there aren't many sites like this on the internet. In fact, Citibank is the only one that I could find. I'm sure that there are others. But they're pretty rare. And so while we might not need to migrate the internet, we might have to ask a few of these sites to use sane practices like not having hundreds of different SSL certificates.
cues.zh: 因此，每次你连接时，都会得到不同的证书，这意味着所有公证人看到的是不同的证书，你的浏览器看到的也是不同的证书，这与遭到攻击的情况看起来一模一样。好消息是，互联网上像这样的网站并不多。事实上，花旗银行是我能找到的唯一一个。我确信还有其他的，但它们非常罕见。所以，虽然我们可能不需要迁移整个互联网，但我们可能需要要求少数这类网站采用合理的做法，比如不要拥有数百个不同的SSL证书。

cues.en: The other problem right now is captive portals. So if you're running convergence right now and you're like in an airport and hotel, you want to connect to the internet and you'll get redirected to this captive portal where you have to type in your credit card number before you can actually access the internet. Now you want to secure this connection with the captive portal, but the captive portal is not letting internet traffic out, so you can't contact your notaries. And so right now you have to actually just unclick convergence in order to deal with this thing.
cues.zh: 现在另一个问题是强制门户。如果你现在运行 convergence，在机场或酒店想连网时，会被重定向到强制门户，得先输入信用卡号才能上网。你想通过强制门户建立安全连接，但强制门户不放行互联网流量，你就联系不上公证人。所以现在只能先取消勾选 convergence 来应付这种情况。

cues.en: But the good news is that almost always in these captive portal situations, they let DNS out, which means that we only have to build a convergence protocol over DNS, and it'll work in a captive portal situation as well. You can download the software. I released it yesterday from convergence.io and tried out. It's in beta. Look at the server stuff. If you want to run a notary. Set one up.
cues.zh: 好消息是，在强制门户场景里几乎总是放行 DNS，这意味着我们只需基于 DNS 构建 convergence 协议，它也能在强制门户下工作。你可以下载软件，我昨天在 convergence.io 发布了，可以试试。还是 beta 版。看看服务端那部分，如果你想运行公证人，就搭一个。

cues.en: Talk to people who might trust you and ask them to configure you as a notary. Even if you're not going to try convergence or you're not into it, the one question that I want to leave you with here today is whenever someone is proposing another authenticity system, I think the question that we should all ask is who do we have to trust and for how long? If the answer is a prescribed set of people forever, proceed with caution. In the meantime, try out convergence.
cues.zh: 跟可能信任你的人聊聊，请他们把你配置成公证人。就算你不打算试 convergence 或对它不感兴趣，今天我想留给你们的一个问题是：每当有人提出又一个真实性系统时，我们该问的是——我们得信任谁，信任多久？如果答案是永远信任一组指定的人，那就谨慎行事。与此同时，试试 convergence 吧。

cues.en: Thank you.
cues.zh: 谢谢。
